**Austrian banking groups join EPI as Wero expands to fifth market**

*Austria's largest banks have become EPI shareholders, extending Wero's account-to-account payment wallet into a ninth-million-population market and reinforcing the initiative's expansion momentum.*

Erste Group, Raiffeisen Bank International and the Austrian savings bank sector have joined the European Payments Initiative as shareholders, bringing Wero to Austria. The move adds a market of roughly nine million potential users to Wero's existing base of 55 million across Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

The Austrian expansion follows Rabobank's recent decision to begin migrating iDEAL transactions to Wero in the Netherlands, a significant operational test for the platform. Austria's addition is notable partly because it brings in banking groups with substantial Central and Eastern European footprints, potentially smoothing future expansion into those markets.

EPI has said it plans to migrate 15 national payment schemes onto Wero over time. Each new market entry tests whether the account-to-account model can displace entrenched domestic schemes and card networks. Austria, where card penetration is lower than in some Western European markets but cash use remains high, presents a different adoption challenge from Wero's initial launch countries.

*Sources: [Austrian banks embrace Wero](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47968/austrian-banks-embrace-wero) — Finextra | [EPI Expands Wero to Austria as Major Banking Groups Join as Shareholders](https://ffnews.com/news/epi-expands-wero-to-austria-as-major-banking-groups-join-as-shareholders) — FF News*

**Volume secures FCA authorisation to operate open banking payments independently**

*Volume Payments has received FCA authorisation as a payment institution, enabling the open banking payment platform to operate under its own licence rather than relying on a third-party provider's permissions.*

Volume, which provides a unified payment platform across bank rails, has been authorised by the FCA as an Authorised Payment Institution. The licence allows Volume to initiate payments and provide payment services directly, rather than operating under the regulatory umbrella of another licensed entity.

The timing is relevant given recent consolidation in UK open banking infrastructure. Neonomics shut down earlier this month, with Access PaySuite acquiring its assets. For firms building on open banking rails, holding a direct FCA licence reduces dependency on third-party providers and the counterparty risk that comes with it. Volume's authorisation positions it among a growing but still relatively small group of open banking-focused firms with their own regulatory standing in the UK market.

*Sources: [Volume secures FCA authorisation](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110204/volume-secures-fca-authorisation) — Finextra*

stories.original:
**Modulr launches commercial variable recurring payments under new UK scheme**

*Modulr has gone live with commercial variable recurring payments, becoming one of the first providers to offer the service under the UK Payments Initiative's new scheme rules.*

Modulr's launch of commercial variable recurring payments follows the UK Payments Initiative's rollout of its VRP scheme earlier this month. Modulr was involved in shaping the scheme as a participant and is now among the first to bring the product to market.

Commercial VRPs extend the open banking payment initiation model beyond the sweeping use case — where VRPs have been live for several years — into merchant payments such as subscriptions, utility bills and other recurring charges. The commercial proposition has been slow to materialise, with years of industry debate about liability frameworks, dispute resolution and the economics of displacing direct debits. Modulr's launch, built on the new centralised scheme rules rather than bilateral agreements, will test whether standardised terms can accelerate adoption where earlier bilateral approaches did not gain traction.

*Sources: [Modulr launches commercial variable recurring payments](https://itbrief.co.uk/story/modulr-launches-commercial-variable-recurring-payments) — IT Brief UK*

stories.original:
**UK fintech sector calls for legislative stability as open finance stalls**

*A bobsguide analysis argues that the UK's transition to open finance and its broader Smart Data economy have slowed materially, hampered by political turnover and insufficient parliamentary time.*

The piece, published by bobsguide, makes the case that six prime ministers in ten years have left UK fintech without the legislative continuity needed to advance frameworks for open banking, digital assets and AI oversight. The transition from open banking to open finance, in particular, has lost momentum as the Data (Use and Access) Bill and related initiatives compete for scarce parliamentary attention.

The argument is not new, but the framing is sharper than usual. The UK's early lead in open banking — built on regulatory mandate rather than legislation — now risks becoming a liability as the next phase requires primary legislation that successive governments have deprioritised. Meanwhile, the EU's PSD3 and Financial Data Access Regulation are advancing through their own legislative processes, and Switzerland recently extended its open finance framework to cover pension data. The UK's position as a regulatory reference point for open finance is eroding through inaction rather than any deliberate policy choice.

*Sources: [Six PMs in ten years - UK fintech needs stability now more than ever](https://www.bobsguide.com/six-pms-in-ten-years-uk-fintech-needs-stability-now-more-than-ever/) — bobsguide*
